sections.h2: How fast can I sell a house in Vancouver, WA?
sections.html:
The pace of a Vancouver sale depends on the buyer's money, the title work and one county step that every Clark County deed passes through. A buyer who pays cash removes the lender from the timeline, which is why owners facing a move, an inherited house or a repair bill often ask for cash offers. A traditional listing adds showings, an appraisal and a loan approval on top.

Vancouver is the seat of Clark County, on the north bank of the Columbia River directly across from Portland. The Census Bureau puts the population at 199,698 as of July 1, 2025, up 4.6 percent from the 2020 base. That growth means plenty of buyers and plenty of investors looking at the same streets you live on, so comparing more than one offer is realistic here.

sections.h2: What do the numbers say about the Vancouver housing market?
sections.html:
Census data gives a baseline for what a typical Vancouver home looks like on paper. The figures below come from the Census Bureau QuickFacts table for Vancouver city.

MeasureVancouver city
Population, July 1, 2025199,698
Owner-occupied housing rate, 2020 to 202450.8%
Median value of owner-occupied homes, 2020 to 2024$462,400
Median gross rent, 2020 to 2024$1,702
Households, 2020 to 202481,504
Mean travel time to work23.2 minutes

With 50.8 percent of homes owner-occupied, about half of Vancouver housing is rented. A house that needs work can interest a landlord or investor as much as a buyer who plans to live in it.

sections.h2: Which parts of Vancouver have the oldest housing?
sections.html:
West Vancouver holds downtown and most of the older parts of the city, while East Vancouver grew after the 1997 annexation, which added 11,258 acres and 58,171 residents. NE Andresen Road is the usual dividing line between the two halves.

Several well-known neighborhoods began as wartime housing. When the Kaiser shipyard drew tens of thousands of workers in the 1940s, the Vancouver Housing Authority was created along with six residential developments: Fruit Valley, Fourth Plain Village, Bagley Downs, Ogden Meadows, Burton Homes and McLoughlin Heights. If your house is in one of those areas, expect a buyer's inspector to look closely at age-related items.

  • Original wiring and panels
  • Galvanized or older supply plumbing
  • Foundations, crawl spaces and drainage
  • Roofs and insulation

More than a third of the Vancouver urban area lives in unincorporated pockets such as Hazel Dell, Felida, Orchards and Salmon Creek, which are outside city limits. Check whether your address is in the city before you look up permit or rental rules, because the city's rules stop at its boundary.

sections.h2: How do Vancouver's weather and river affect a house?
sections.html:
Vancouver has a warm-summer Mediterranean climate with about 42 inches of precipitation a year. Rain is frequent from fall through spring and tapers off around mid June, so roofs, gutters and crawl spaces take most of the wear. Cold east winds funnel down the Columbia River Gorge, and the city has seen freezing-rain storms that coat trees and power lines in ice.

The Columbia has flooded the area before, with destructive events in June 1894 and May 1948, though dams have since narrowed the river's swings. Tornadoes have also touched the metro area, including an EF1 that crossed from Vancouver Lake toward Hazel Dell on January 10, 2008. A buyer's inspector will look hardest at the roof, gutters and crawl space, so those are the places to check before you set a price.

sections.h2: What employers, schools and roads matter to Vancouver buyers?
sections.html:
Health care leads local employment. According to the city's 2022 financial report as summarized on Wikipedia, PeaceHealth is the largest employer with 16,500 employees, followed by Vancouver Public Schools, Evergreen Public Schools, The Vancouver Clinic and Battle Ground Public Schools.

Schools are a selling point in two main districts. Vancouver Public Schools covers most of west Vancouver, and Evergreen Public Schools covers most of the east side. Small portions of the city fall in the Camas and Battle Ground districts, so confirm the district for your exact address.

Commuting shapes demand. Interstates 5 and 205 both cross the Columbia into Portland, SR 14 runs east from downtown, and SR 500 links I-5 to I-205. Rush-hour traffic is heavy on the Interstate Bridge and the Glenn Jackson Bridge, and C-Tran runs local and express bus service. Homes near the freeways often draw commuters who value the shorter trip.

sections.h2: Do I need a permit before selling a Vancouver house?
sections.html:
You need one only if you plan to do the work yourself before closing. The City of Vancouver requires a residential building permit for the construction, alteration, addition, repair or demolition of residential buildings.

The city's residential permit page lists projects that need one:

  • Additions and remodels
  • Adding a garage, carport, deck or patio cover
  • Adding or removing walls
  • Converting a basement, attic or garage into living space
  • Changing the footprint of a structure

Small stand-alone electrical, mechanical or plumbing jobs fall under a trade permit instead. If you suspect past work was done without a permit, the city offers a field evaluation permit, where inspectors decide what permits and corrections are needed. Tree removal also needs a city permit. The Permit Center can be reached at 360-487-7833 for questions.

The city's updated zoning code took effect on July 31, 2026, and it allows more middle housing, up to six units on one lot. A buyer with development plans may value a lot differently than a buyer who wants to move in.

sections.h2: What changes if the Vancouver house is a rental?
sections.html:
Landlords selling in city limits should know about two programs. Since January 1, 2026, owners of residential rentals in Vancouver must register each unit every year, at $30 per unit. The free 90-day window closed on March 31, 2026. Health and safety inspections are planned to begin in mid 2027.

The city's rental registration page covers the sale of a registered rental: the registration must be transferred to the new owner within 60 days of the property transfer, with no extra fee. If you stop renting, you can deregister the property. Questions go to rentalregistration@cityofvancouver.us or 360-487-7928.

Short-term rentals are a separate permit. Vancouver defines one as a rental of fewer than 30 consecutive nights, and the permit requires a Washington business license with the city endorsement, at least $1 million in liability insurance and a notice mailed to abutting neighbors. The city caps total permits at 870, or about 1 percent of its housing stock. A permit does not override a lease or homeowners association rules, so a buyer who plans to use the house this way should confirm the status with the city's short-term rental page.

sections.h2: How do the deed and excise tax work in Clark County?
sections.html:
Every Clark County sale runs through the Treasurer first and the Auditor second. The Treasurer collects the real estate excise tax, and under RCW 82.45.090 the Auditor cannot accept a deed for recording until that tax is paid or the Treasurer notes that none is due.

The Clark County Treasurer states that the tax is due 30 days from the date of sale and that a $5 processing fee is added. The state part is graduated by sale price:

  • 1.10 percent on a price up to $525,000
  • 1.28 percent from $525,000.01 to $1,525,000
  • 2.75 percent from $1,525,000.01 to $3,025,000
  • 3.00 percent above $3,025,000

A local rate is added on top, so ask the Treasurer or your closing agent for the total on your price. In person, the office is at 1300 Franklin Street, 2nd Floor, Monday to Thursday from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. After payment, the Auditor's Recording Department at the same address records the deed. Its recording guide lists 564-397-2208 for questions.

Washington also requires the seller of improved residential property to deliver a disclosure statement under RCW 64.06.020, normally within five business days after the contract is accepted. The buyer then has three business days after delivery to rescind unless both sides agree otherwise.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Vancouver, WA house as-is?
faqs.a: Yes, a house can be sold in its current condition. You still owe the buyer the state seller disclosure statement for improved residential property under RCW 64.06.020, and any unpermitted work you know about belongs in it.

faqs.q: Who records the deed when a Vancouver house sells?
faqs.a: The Clark County Auditor's Recording Department records it, but only after the Treasurer's Office handles the excise tax affidavit. Both offices are at 1300 Franklin Street, and title or escrow companies normally submit the paperwork for you.

faqs.q: What happens to my Vancouver rental registration when I sell?
faqs.a: It transfers to the new owner. The city says the registration must be moved within 60 days of the property transfer, and there is no additional fee. If the buyer will live in the home, the registration can be ended through deregistration.

faqs.q: Does Vancouver cap short-term rental permits?
faqs.a: Yes. The city limits permits to 870, or about 1 percent of its total housing stock. Anyone buying a house to run as a short-term rental should check permit availability with the Permit Center before paying a premium for that use.

faqs.q: Which school district is my Vancouver house in?
faqs.a: Most of west Vancouver is in Vancouver Public Schools and most of east Vancouver is in Evergreen Public Schools. Small portions are in the Camas and Battle Ground districts, so check the address with the district before you describe it to a buyer.
